method_card.title: Bar Charts, Pie Charts and Stem-and-Leaf Diagrams
method_card.content:
A pie chart represents data as sectors of a circle. The formula for each sector angle is given on the formula sheet: \(\text{angle} = \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total}} \times 360\). Always divide by the total frequency, not by the number of categories.

A comparative pie chart uses two circles of different sizes to compare two datasets. The areas of the circles are proportional to the totals, so a dataset with twice the total has a circle with \(\sqrt{2}\) times the radius — not twice the radius. This is a Higher-tier skill.

For a stem-and-leaf diagram, the stem is the leading digit(s) and the leaf is the final digit. Always include a key (e.g. 3 | 7 means 37). A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram places two datasets either side of a shared stem, allowing direct comparison of shape, median and spread.

Bar charts come in several forms: a dual bar chart places two bars side by side for direct comparison. A composite (stacked) bar chart stacks bars to show both the total and the component parts. A percentage bar chart standardises all bars to 100%, removing the effect of different group sizes.

When reading a Venn diagram, the intersection represents items in both categories. P(A ∩ B) is read from the overlapping region; P(A only) excludes the intersection. Count carefully and always check whether the question asks for a count or a probability.
steps: For a pie sector angle, divide the category frequency by the total, then multiply by 360
For a stem-and-leaf diagram, split each value into its stem (leading digit) and leaf (final digit)
Write the key for any stem-and-leaf diagram (e.g. 2 | 4 means 24)
For back-to-back diagrams, read left-side leaves from right to left (they still increase outward from the stem)
For a Venn diagram, identify the intersection, left-only, right-only and outside regions before answering any question
For comparative pie charts (Higher), check whether you are being asked to compare angles or actual frequencies

exam_context.marks: 2–5 marks; sector angle calculations are 2 marks, back-to-back stem-and-leaf comparisons up to 4 marks
exam_context.frequency: Pie chart sector angles and stem-and-leaf reading appear on most papers; Venn diagram intersection questions appear on roughly half of all papers

worked_examples.question: 30 students were asked their favourite subject. 12 chose Maths. What angle is needed for the Maths sector in a pie chart?

A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows test scores for two classes. Class A (left): stem 5 has leaves 9, 8, 3; stem 6 has leaves 7, 2; stem 7 has leaves 5, 1. Class B (right): stem 5 has leaves 1, 4; stem 6 has leaves 0, 6, 8; stem 7 has leaves 3, 7, 9. Find the median for each class.

steps.label: Step 1 — List Class A values in order
Step 2 — List Class B values in order
steps.content: 51, 54, 60, 66, 68, 73, 77, 79 — 8 values, median is the mean of the 4th and 5th: \(\frac{66 + 68}{2} = 67\)

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Class A median = 62; Class B median = 67. Class B scored higher on average.

worked_examples.question: A Venn diagram shows 40 students. 24 study History, 18 study Geography, and 8 study both. How many students study neither subject? What is the probability a randomly chosen student studies History only?

steps.label: Step 1 — Find History only and Geography only
Step 2 — Find those studying at least one subject
steps.content: \(16 + 10 + 8 = 34\) students study at least one subject.

steps.label: Step 3 — Find neither and the probability
Answer
steps.content: 6 students study neither subject. P(History only) = 2/5.

bronze.display: A survey of 60 people found 15 preferred tea. What angle represents the tea sector in a pie chart?

misconceptions.message: Angle = (15/60) × 360 = 0.25 × 360 = 90°. Divide by the total (60), not the number of categories.

bronze.display: A pie chart sector for 'Cycling' has an angle of 72°. The pie chart represents 100 people in total. How many people chose cycling?

misconceptions.message: Frequency = (72/360) × 100 = 0.2 × 100 = 20. Reverse the sector-angle formula.

bronze.display: A stem-and-leaf diagram has key: 4 | 7 means 47. The stem 3 row has leaves 2, 5, 8, 8. What is the largest value in the stem 3 row?

misconceptions.message: Stem 3 with leaf 8 means 38. The leaves are individual digits appended to the stem.

bronze.display: A dual bar chart shows sales for two shops in January and February. Shop A January: 40 units; Shop B January: 55 units. How many more units did Shop B sell than Shop A in January?

misconceptions.message: 55 − 40 = 15 units. Read each bar from zero.

bronze.display: A pie chart has four sectors with angles 90°, 120°, 80°, and x°. Find x.
A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram is described as showing the ages of members in two clubs. Which property can be directly compared from a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram?
options: The range and median of both datasets simultaneously
The mean of both datasets without any calculation
The exact variance of each dataset
The cumulative frequency of each dataset

misconceptions.message: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf shows the shape, spread (range) and middle value (median) visually for both sets at once. It does not give the mean directly — that requires calculation.

bronze.display: 48 students were surveyed. 20 play a team sport, 15 do an individual sport, and 7 do both. How many students do neither?

misconceptions.message: Team only: 20 − 7 = 13. Individual only: 15 − 7 = 8. In at least one: 13 + 8 + 7 = 28. Neither: 48 − 28 = 20.

bronze.display: A pie chart is drawn for the following data: Red: 18, Blue: 12, Green: 6, Yellow: 4. What is the total frequency?

misconceptions.message: Total = 18 + 12 + 6 + 4 = 40. You must find this total before calculating any sector angle.

silver.display: A survey of 45 students found: 18 prefer football, 12 prefer tennis, 9 prefer swimming, 6 prefer other. Calculate the sector angle for the swimming category.

misconceptions.message: Angle = (9/45) × 360 = 0.2 × 360 = 72°. Divide by total 45, not by any other value.

silver.display: A stem-and-leaf diagram for 9 values has key 2 | 3 means 23. Stems and leaves: 1 | 5, 8; 2 | 0, 3, 7; 3 | 1, 4, 9. Key: 2 | 3 means 23. Find the median.

misconceptions.message: 9 values ordered: 15, 18, 20, 23, 27, 31, 34, 39. The median is the 5th value: 23. You must read the leaves in order, not just pick the middle row.

silver.display: A composite (stacked) bar chart shows two products. Product A: 30 sold online, 20 sold in-store (total bar height = 50). Product B: 45 sold online, 15 sold in-store (total bar height = 60). What percentage of Product B's sales were in-store?

misconceptions.message: In-store for B = 15, total for B = 60. Percentage = (15/60) × 100 = 25%. Do not use Product A's total.

silver.display: In a Venn diagram of 50 students, 30 own a dog (D) and 22 own a cat (C). 8 own both. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student owns a cat but not a dog?

misconceptions.message: Cat only = 22 − 8 = 14. P(cat only) = 14/50 = 7/25. The denominator is the total 50, not just those owning cats.

silver.display: A percentage bar chart shows two year groups. Year 10: 40% achieved grade 4+; Year 11: 65% achieved grade 4+. Year 10 has 120 students and Year 11 has 80 students. How many more Year 10 students than Year 11 students achieved grade 4+?

misconceptions.message: Year 10: 40% of 120 = 48. Year 11: 65% of 80 = 52. Difference = 48 − 52 = −4, so Year 11 has 4 more. If the question asks 'how many more Year 10', the answer is 0 (they have 4 fewer). Check the direction of the comparison.
Don't compare percentages directly when group sizes differ. Always calculate the actual counts first.

silver.display: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows times (in minutes) for two runners. Runner A stems 2 | leaves 3, 7, 9; stem 3 | leaves 1, 5; stem 4 | leaves 0. Runner B stem 2 | leaves 1, 5; stem 3 | leaves 0, 2, 8; stem 4 | leaves 4, 6. Key: 3 | 1 means 31 minutes. Which runner has the smaller range?

misconceptions.message: Runner A: min = 23, max = 40, range = 17. Runner B: min = 21, max = 46, range = 25. Always read the leaves from smallest to largest when finding the min and max.

gold.display: A survey of 80 people asked about two streaming services. 52 use Service A, 45 use Service B, and 28 use both. How many use neither service?
A pie chart represents 120 people. The sector for 'Bus' has angle 75°. How many people chose Bus?

misconceptions.message: Frequency = (75/360) × 120 = 0.2083 × 120 = 25. Reverse the formula: frequency = (angle/360) × total.

gold.display: Two datasets are displayed in a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram. Dataset X has 9 values; Dataset Y has 9 values. Dataset X (left, read right to left from stem): stem 4 | leaves 8, 5, 2; stem 5 | leaves 9, 3, 1; stem 6 | leaves 7, 4, 0. Dataset Y (right from stem): stem 4 | leaves 1, 6, 9; stem 5 | leaves 0, 4, 7; stem 6 | leaves 2, 5, 8. Find the interquartile range of Dataset X.

misconceptions.message: X ordered: 42, 45, 48, 51, 53, 59, 60, 64, 67. n=9. Q1 = 2nd value = 45, Q3 = 8th value = 64. IQR = 64 − 45 = 19. Re-check: for n=9 (one less than a multiple of 4, here 8+1), Q1 is the (9+1)/4 = 2.5th position → average 2nd and 3rd: (45+48)/2 = 46.5. Q3 at 3(9+1)/4 = 7.5th: (60+64)/2 = 62. IQR = 62 − 46.5 = 15.5. Use the AQA n=one-less-than-multiple-of-4 rule carefully.
Read Dataset X leaves from right to left (they increase outward from the stem). The values are 42, 45, 48, 51, 53, 59, 60, 64, 67 — not the mirror image.

gold.display: A composite bar chart has three categories (A, B, C) stacked. Category A is always the bottom segment. For Group 1 the total bar is 80, with A = 30 and B = 25. For Group 2 the total bar is 60, with A = 24 and B = 18. What percentage of Group 1's bar is taken up by segment C?

misconceptions.message: Group 1 C = 80 − 30 − 25 = 25. Percentage = (25/80) × 100 = 31.25%. Find segment C's frequency first, then divide by the total for that group.

gold.display: A Venn diagram shows 3 events. Event M, Event N, and Event P (all within a sample space of 100 outcomes). M only: 20; N only: 15; P only: 25; M ∩ N only: 8; M ∩ P only: 6; N ∩ P only: 4; M ∩ N ∩ P: 3. How many outcomes are in none of the three events?

misconceptions.message: In a three-circle Venn diagram, each pairwise intersection (e.g. M ∩ N only) does NOT include the triple intersection. The values given are for each distinct region, so add them all before subtracting from the total.
